reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Facial fractures often accompany high-energy trauma, so assessment follows trauma principles with airway, cervical spine, and associated head and neck injuries addressed first
Midface fractures are classically described by the Le Fort patterns (I, II, III) reflecting different levels of maxillary separation, and higher patterns can produce a mobile or displaced midface
Zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures may cause flattening of the cheek, trismus, altered infraorbital sensation, and a step at the orbital rim
Orbital floor (blowout) fractures can trap the inferior rectus and cause diplopia, restricted upgaze, enophthalmos, and infraorbital numbness
Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea, a nasoethmoidal injury, or telecanthus points to fractures extending toward the skull base and cribriform region
CT of the facial skeleton is the imaging standard for defining fracture patterns and planning reconstruction
Treatment principles are restoring facial height, width, and projection, re-establishing occlusion, and rigid fixation of key buttresses, with surgery timed once swelling allows
A dental and occlusal assessment is essential, as restoring the pre-injury bite guides reduction of maxillary and mandibular fractures
reference.pathophysiology: The facial skeleton is organised into vertical and horizontal buttresses that transmit and dissipate forces of mastication and absorb trauma. Fractures occur when applied force exceeds bone strength, and the pattern reflects the direction and energy of impact and the relative weakness of certain regions such as the orbital floor and the Le Fort lines. High-energy injuries can separate the midface from the skull base along these predictable planes. Associated soft tissue swelling, haemorrhage, and displaced bone fragments can compromise the airway, the orbit and globe, cranial nerves, and the lacrimal and paranasal sinus systems, and disruption near the cribriform plate can breach the dura and cause CSF leak.
additionalDifferentials: Dentoalveolar injury without facial skeleton fracture
Traumatic globe injury or retrobulbar haemorrhage
Temporal bone or skull base fracture
Soft tissue contusion and haematoma without fracture
additionalInvestigations: CT of the facial skeleton with fine cuts and three-dimensional reconstruction
Ophthalmological assessment including visual acuity and forced duction testing when orbital involvement is suspected
Assessment for CSF rhinorrhoea (e.g. beta-2 transferrin) with suspected skull base extension
Dental and occlusal evaluation, with panoramic imaging for the mandible
Cranial nerve and infraorbital sensory examination
Trauma workup including cervical spine imaging and evaluation for head injury
redFlags: Airway compromise from midface instability, haemorrhage, or swelling, particularly with high Le Fort injuries (emergency)
Visual loss, a tense proptotic orbit, or suspected retrobulbar haemorrhage requiring urgent decompression
Orbital fracture with a trapped muscle and the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea) in children
CSF rhinorrhoea or other evidence of skull base and dural breach
Associated cervical spine or intracranial injury
reference.prognosis: With accurate reduction and fixation most facial fractures heal with good functional and aesthetic results and restored occlusion. Outcomes are less favourable with delayed treatment, comminution, or associated orbital and skull base injury, where diplopia, enophthalmos, malunion, sensory disturbance, and asymmetry may persist and require secondary correction.
pitfalls: Focusing on obvious facial injury while missing airway compromise or cervical spine injury
Overlooking an orbital floor fracture with entrapment, especially the white-eyed blowout in children
Failing to detect and manage CSF leak in fractures extending to the skull base
Neglecting occlusion, resulting in malocclusion after fixation
Operating before periorbital swelling settles, compromising assessment and fixation
Missing retrobulbar haemorrhage, which can cause preventable blindness
management: Trauma primary survey first, securing the airway with cervical-spine protection, controlling haemorrhage and excluding concurrent head and neck injury
CT of the facial skeleton to define the fracture pattern and plan reconstruction
Open reduction and internal fixation of displaced fractures, restoring the facial buttresses and dental occlusion
Orbital floor reconstruction with release of an entrapped inferior rectus in blowout fractures causing diplopia or enophthalmos
Antibiotic prophylaxis for fractures communicating with the sinuses or oral cavity, tetanus cover, and neurosurgical input with management of CSF rhinorrhoea when the skull base is breached
Urgent ophthalmology assessment, with lateral canthotomy for orbital compartment syndrome or retrobulbar haemorrhage threatening the globe
Multidisciplinary reconstruction involving maxillofacial and plastic surgery, ophthalmology, ENT and dental rehabilitation

Displaced fracture or orbital entrapment on CT?
